questions.question: Identify the economically marginalised groups with the mechanism of exclusion in each case, and explain why repealing discriminatory laws did not restore economic equality.
questions.expected_answer: Black South Africans — dispossessed of land by law, restricted in residence, trade and property, denied equal education, channelled into low-wage migrant labour. Women, especially Black women — excluded by law and custom from property, credit and occupations, carrying unpaid care work, still concentrated in lower-paid positions. Rural communities — areas deliberately starved of infrastructure and investment. People with disabilities — physical and attitudinal barriers to schooling and workplaces. Youth — inheriting disadvantage as first-time seekers in a labour market with few entry points. The categories overlap and compound. Repeal stopped the machine but did not undo what it built: disadvantage transmits across generations through assets, education, networks and address, so legal equality and economic equality are different statements.

questions.question: Explain redress through each factor of production, naming what was denied, the instrument, and the support the instrument needs.
questions.expected_answer: Natural resources/land — dispossession answered by restitution (return or compensation for post-1913 dispossession), redistribution (access for those who had none) and tenure reform (securing insecure occupation); support needed: finance, training, equipment and market access, since land without support produces neither livelihood nor output. Labour — job reservation and unequal schooling answered by employment equity (targeting management and skilled levels where exclusion was sharpest) and skills development through levy-funded learnerships and apprenticeships. Capital — exclusion from ownership and credit answered by B-BBEE ownership, management control, enterprise and supplier development and preferential procurement, plus development finance for those without collateral. Entrepreneurship — legal and capital barriers answered by small business support, incubation, simplified regulation, market access and procurement set-asides.

questions.question: Describe the democratisation of economic decision-making, and judge redress on both ledgers.
questions.expected_answer: Democratisation: labour legislation makes workers parties to decisions rather than subjects of them; public hearings and participation give affected people channels into parliamentary, municipal and regulatory decisions; NEDLAC brings government, organised business, organised labour and organised community to one table so major economic policy and labour legislation are negotiated before Parliament — with the limits that consensus is slow and poorly organised constituencies are under-represented; self-regulating professional and industry bodies set and enforce standards inside a legal framework. Judgement: achievements include vastly expanded access to services, housing, education and grants, a substantial Black middle and professional class, shifted ownership and management demographics, and protective law and institutions; shortfalls include persistently high unemployment, extreme inequality, slow and often unsupported land reform, and benefits sometimes concentrated among a narrow elite — the critique 'broad-based' answers. State both ledgers with mechanisms, distinguishing evidence from preference.
